speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You see the details in the Green Paper that has been filed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It gives a framework for the Government’s reasons for bringing this Motion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And the Green Paper sets out in a summary some of the more serious ones.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, of course, the very high Internet penetration in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: More than 91% of Singaporean households have Internet access.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it is easy to attack and spread falsehoods in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Second, our diversity − as a multi-racial, multi-religious society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That makes it easy to exploit the fault-lines through falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, in June of last year, that cat and dog meat were mixed into a marinade of satay in a Geylang bazaar.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is a relatively minor example, though it can make a lot of people very angry.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But you have more serious examples from other countries.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You see some of them in the Green Paper.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: People can and have targeted specific sections of populations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: They can target specific sections of our population − using falsehoods based on race, religion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Third, our international position, both in this region and internationally, makes us an attractive target.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are a key strategic node, a key player in ASEAN.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We are a trade hub, commercial hub, financial hub for this entire region.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What we say on regional issues and international issues carries weight.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if we can be influenced and swayed, then foreign interests can be advanced through us.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: We have been the subject of foreign interference in the past.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, a Malaysian politician financing a newspaper in Singapore which campaigns against National Service – you cannot get a more obvious example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, technology has added a completely new dimension.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister Yaacob will touch on the points relating to technology and how it has completely changed the landscape.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Wide spreading of falsehoods can drown out the facts, can cause people to be disillusioned, can be manipulated to create rifts and damage social cohesion.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the people who shout loudest and shout falsehoods are those who will get hurt.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Falsehoods, because they tend to be focused on playing to people's feelings and getting them to be angry by putting forward points which are completely fabricated.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A very senior officer in Sweden is reported by BBC to have said – and this was reported last week – disinformation as a tool, as a campaign, in the context of Sweden has had effect.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It affects Sweden's "fundamental values: freedom of speech, democracy and individual rights".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government has been studying this problem for a while.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Select Committee can study the issue in depth with a smaller group of Members of Parliament (MPs), and then present a report to Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It will be open to the Select Committee to decide whether to hold public hearings, whether to hear from witnesses.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think it will be useful to do so.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The process will allow for a formal dialogue with selected groups.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, we will have − eight Government MPs, one opposition MP and one NMP.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Select Committee will have to consider relevant views and options.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: More fundamentally, it is about maintaining our sovereignty, as well as the multi-racial nature of our society, by ensuring that those who wish to do us harm by peddling falsehoods online do not succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: As we have seen in other countries, deliberate campaigns to proliferate falsehoods online have caused panic and confusion, worsened societal fault-lines and eroded trust in public institutions.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: If unchecked, they may result in grave consequences for the country's social and political discourse.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Let us not forget that Singapore has fallen victim to foreign interference through falsehood and misinformation before.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Mr Shanmugam just spoke about the Singapore Herald's misinformation and campaign in the early-1970s.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The funds were provided on the condition that they would not post the People's Republic of China on major issues and publish news items of the communists' choice.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, we were fortunate to nip this in the bud early enough, so that this campaign did not sink our young nation back in the day.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But today, such orchestrated campaigns can wreck even more harm.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In the Internet age, falsehoods can go viral in seconds.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Digital content can be easily manipulated to make it more provocative and stir emotions more easily.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Anyone can publish or share falsehoods online, even from halfway around the world.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: And the net result is that online falsehoods can destabilise societies far more easily than ever before.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Take, for example, the example of the now defunct, The Real Singaporean or TRS website, which my Ministry shut down in May 2015.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: TRS published doctored articles which sensational headlines as clickbait to increase traffic to its website so as to inflate its readership and earn more advertising dollars.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In February 2015, TRS published a false article on a Filipino family complaining about the noise from a Thaipusam procession involving Indian Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The article was deliberately fabricated and falsely attributed the incident to innocent parties to fuel anti-foreigner sentiments.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It went viral and created tensions between our local Indian community and the Filipinos living in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Fortunately, we acted swiftly to prevent TRS from doing further harm.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: In the United Kingdom (UK), foreign Twitter accounts posted four tweets in the month leading up to the UK Referendum, such as how millions of Turkish people will move to the UK, if the UK voted to remain in the European Union (EU).

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Such falsehoods aimed to influence voters and the outcomes of elections.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: These outcomes in some cases changed the course of the countries, like what Brexit appears to have done.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: But let me clarify that we are not against technology.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: It is the people and actors abusing technology to spread online falsehoods that are the problem.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: And indeed, technology has improved our lives in many ways, and while technology can be used to divide societies, so too can it be used to bring people together, such as by connecting communities across the world, or mobilising volunteers during crises.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: That said, as technology continues to push the frontiers of reality, it will be easier to create false information and damage societies.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: So, for instance, in 2016, Professors at Stanford University and the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg demonstrated how technologies can record a video of people tin real-time, effectively manipulating their expressions to reflect the message the perpetrators want to convey.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Adobe launched a new product in 2016 called "Photoshop for Audio", which allows users to feed about 10 to 20 minutes of someone's voice into an application.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The user then type any words he or she wants to say, which will be expressed in the same exact voice.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: The resultant voice sounds virtually indistinguishable from the real and does not sound computer-generated at all.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: This can be used to impersonate anyone, even Heads of States.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Singapore is especially vulnerable to this for several reasons.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: First, we are a small and multi-racial society that can be easily overwhelmed by a larger adversary, taking advantage of our societal fault-lines.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Second, Singapore has one of the highest smartphone penetration rates in the world at almost 150%.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: People can easily access the Internet and social media on their smartphones anytime and anywhere, and hence, are more susceptible to the spread of online falsehoods.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: And third, while we have a population that is technology-savvy, it is an entirely different matter, whether we have the ability discern truth from falsehood.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Two in three of them were unable to recognise some or all of the falsities.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: And one in four admitted to sharing news that they later found was fake.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: Organisations, such as the Media Literary Council and Government agencies like the NLB, have developed programmes and resources to raise public standards of media literacy.

speaker: The Minister for Communications and Information (Assoc Prof Dr Yaacob Ibrahim)
text: While public education remains our first line of defence, it is not enough.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have heard from the Ministers why deliberate online falsehoods have become a global problem.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have one of the highest levels of Internet penetration in the world.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have an active, well-read and inquisitive population.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We have ready access to information, across borders, across time, across languages.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can read and write all sorts of things online.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But these very strengths can also be used against us, when we face the onslaught of online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Everything that the world faces, we can face here, in a quicker time, with a nearer striking distance.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Given how small we are, falsehoods can spread online in seconds, reaching a large segment of population and causing great inconvenience to everyone.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: When false news of the roof collapse at Waterway Terraces I, which is in my ward, broke, I was on the phone in seconds calling up the Town Council, calling up my grassroots leaders to rush there as soon as they can while I drive there from another part of town.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The false news was taken down in half an hour but many things happened within that half hour.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Singapore Police Force (SPF) and Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) despatched vehicles and manpower.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other residents texted to say that they were rushing home.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: And even after the news was taken down, to play safe, I still mobilised the Town Council to go around check for cracks on walls.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: So, this might be someone’s idea of a joke, but it was not a very efficient use of time and resources.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Because of how small Singapore is and how connected we are, we can mobilise quickly to respond to situations.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: In the example that I just provided, everyone was rushing to the scene to provide help.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: But what if our speed and proximity instead ended up harming us?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Recently, in Wichita Kansas, an innocent man was shot dead by the police after pranksters called the police to say that he had shot one of his family members and was holding the rest of them hostage.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The police SWAT team responded quickly and in force, went down to his doorstep and shot him dead at his doorstep.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It is also not altogether unimaginable if online falsehoods on a financial institution were put up, leading to a bank run or if someone wanted to agitate foreign workers in Singapore and put up something to say that Singaporeans bullied them.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Foreign agents and organisations have been identified as seeding fake news to attack these large countries.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We should not think that we are immune to this.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Rivalry between states have existed since time immemorial.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore though small, is a key player in ASEAN and a key node for trade, finance and communications.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Foreign powers to advance their interests in the region may seek to manipulate Singapore from within, through the seeding of deliberate online falsehoods, injecting ideas, narrow casting to groups split along racial, religious, or along ideological lines.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Such insidious actions can polarise our society, erode the middle ground and destabilise us.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we take a big stick and censor all information online?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That would be akin to throwing the baby out with the bathwater.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our openness and access to information is one of our key strengths and has played a key role in creating a thriving and international city out of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Do we legislate laws to tackle online falsehoods?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: It sounds reasonable to penalise those who choose to act irresponsibly and deliberately spread online falsehoods and to create safeguards to ensure that that does not happen.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we distinguish those who knowingly create or spread online falsehood from those who are just expressing their opinions?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How do we ensure that legislating laws to tackle online falsehood will not end up impeding our right to free speech?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Or is part of the solution also to encourage greater media literacy in our citizens, so that they can discern truth from falsehood and working with technology companies to use algorithms to distil facts from fiction?

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I worry about relying solely on the efforts of companies to self-regulate or putting the onus of responsibility on citizens to discern truth from falsehood because if that alone were enough, we would not see online falsehoods proliferating and affecting so many countries worldwide.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: That said, I believe the Motion proposed by the Minister to have a Select Committee examine and report on the problems posed by online falsehood and various ways to tackle them is a worthwhile step forward.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I am supportive of the broadly drafted terms of reference – they reflect the fact that the Select Committee will be considering all options, fairly and objectively.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I would, however, like to ask the Minister how the Select Committee will be organised, how views will be sought and how the public can participate in the process.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I think it is important that there is: (a) a thorough discussion of the problems posed by deliberate online falsehoods, (b) that the process is inclusive so that representations can be received from all sectors and stakeholders and we benefit from their opinions and breadth of knowledge; (c) that there is ample time for questions to be asked and clarifications provided; and (d) that all options are considered and the recommendations are something that Singaporeans can read for themselves and consider for themselves.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This should be a study that the Government, Singaporeans and companies embark on together to find solutions to combat deliberate online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: (In Mandarin):   Through public voting, Lianhe Zaobao readers selected the word "terror" to describe the year 2017.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This is not accidental, as there were many terror attacks all over the world last year.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Besides terror attacks, there is another weapon which can also cause fear and anxiety in society and destroy social cohesion.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This weapon is more insidious and harmful in the long term, but it is often overlooked by people.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: False news can spread in seconds to a large population and pose a major hidden danger for the society.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We can imagine what would happen if the false news is not about a collapsed roof but about credit issue of a bank.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: If the depositors or investors see the false news and a run-on-the-bank happens, the bank will then close down, resulting in real capital loss.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Deliberate false news is harmful for the economy and people's lives.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A new word has emerged these days called "post-truth politics" to describe a situation whereby the real truth does not matter anymore and that the situation is driven by people's emotions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: The Oxford Dictionary has even listed the word as a key word for 2016, which shows how widespread this phenomenon has become internationally.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: False news is the key instrument to incite people's feelings and create post-truth politics.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: False news can target a certain community or race in society, instil racial and religious ideology, and breed extremist ideas.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: This kind of slow and subtle influence can lead to a social divide and affect social stability.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore, although small, is a key player in ASEAN and a key node for trade, finance and communications.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To advance their interests in the region, foreign powers may seek to manipulate Singapore through these means.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Internationally, there are already people using the Internet to interfere with other countries' politics.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They tend to possess powerful resources and advanced Internet technology.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They can fabricate false news to infuriate people in another country, cause domestic turmoil and may even influence regime change.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Singapore must stay vigilant so that these people will not succeed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: For insidious false news, we cannot sit around to be fooled and harmed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We need to build our own defence system.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many countries in the world face the same difficult issue and still there are no good solutions.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: We cannot rely solely on the efforts of companies to self-regulate, because there may be people who profit from fabricating false news.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Neither can we put the onus on citizens to separate truth from falsehood.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To prevent false news from harming the society, we should consider legislation.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: However, we should also be mindful, when legislating laws, that we do not take away citizens' right to free speech.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: I hope the Committee can conduct comprehensive public consultations to allow people to participate in the discussions and allow all sectors to give their views.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: At the same time, we need ample time for questions to be asked and discussed.

speaker: Ms Sun Xueling (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Lastly, I hope that we can find a solution that will benefit Singapore and Singaporeans, a workable solution which is achieved through discussions among all Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For as long as human societies existed, there would always be incidence of rumours, untruths being spread in various media.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Such falsehoods affect people, relationships, the way people see things, and ultimately, impacts on the society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Human societies have managed to cope and deal with such incidents and its consequences.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, with the advent of digital technology, the spread of falsehoods and its impact on communities have reached unprecedented levels.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The spread of deliberate online falsehood is, therefore, of particular concern.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are now many more information systems and platforms which translates to more means and ways by which falsehoods can be spread.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: With the proliferation via social media, falsehoods spread much faster.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We now have the concept of "going viral", a problem which we never had to deal with before.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There is now instant communication – Twitter, Facebook Messenger, Instagram, Telegram – and with a click of a button, an individual could share information to many others almost immediately.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On Facebook, an individual could share a post to 5,000 people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: On a single WhatsApp group, you can have up to 256 members.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Imagine the extent of the reach in numerous WhatsApp groups.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is natural for people who think alike to come together and share views.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Internet has made it easier for us to talk amongst ourselves with people of like-minded views.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In such context, we end up confirming each other’s pre-existing views and reinforce our own biases.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Often in such groups, there is no other source of information coming into our circle.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We therefore form echo chambers and this amplifies the impact of any falsehoods spread within the group.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Thirdly, there are people taking advantage of the new means of human communication and the human psyche to spread falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The identities of those creating or proliferating falsehoods online are hidden behind the screen of anonymity, such that they are emboldened to spread the falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There have been and will continue to be unsavoury people who would use the online platforms to propagate falsehoods for their own desirable ends and to pursue their own agendas.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, it is observed that in many places, the mainstream media no longer holds the same degree of trust it had with the people.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The people have a preference to refer to sources, other than the mainstream media.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The mainstream media now operates in a different environment where it can no longer operate as an effective check and balance on the proliferation of online falsehoods, enabled by technology and social media.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe we can all appreciate the significant adverse impact online falsehoods can have on communities.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Just look at the buzz that was caused when many people received the message that NTUC FairPrice was giving out gift cards.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: A friend said that she saw a lady insisting for a gift card at one of the outlets.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: For example, when terror attacks occurred in Paris in November 2015, a video went viral claiming that London Muslims were celebrating the attacks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In reality, it was a video of a celebration of a victory by Pakistan in a cricket match.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The hoax fed into the anger against Muslims in the aftermath of the Paris attacks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As a Muslim minority in Singapore, I cringe every time I hear news of terror attacks.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I always worry about the distrust that could develop against the Muslims in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is one of my greatest fears that an online falsehood could trigger anger against the Muslim community here.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There could be disastrous implications if this happens in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The problem of the spread of online falsehoods is a very real problem and merits immediate attention.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: So, we know the problem, but what do we do about it?

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are numerous ways to address the spread of online falsehoods but the current measures appear inadequate.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Currently, there are statutes like the Telecommunications Act and the Broadcasting Act, which may apply but there are gaps.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The circulation of falsehoods is hard to circumvent, given how quickly they go viral today.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One person could possibly be held accountable under the statute for sending the message containing the falsehood but its virulent spread thereafter, cannot be adequately dealt with using existing provisions in law.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The technology companies are also making effort to take steps to stop the spread of falsehoods by flagging information to consumers or by taking down the posts which breach community standards.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, researchers subsequently highlighted to Facebook that this method is ineffective as it was actually entrenching deeply held beliefs.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, Facebook will no longer display these red warning icons but instead display links to related articles next to the disputed news stories.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: There are also some ground-up efforts of fact-checking that are emerging.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This is an encouraging effort, but I believe it is still too early to tell how successful this will be in the fight against online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The reality is that existing measures and efforts are not able to curb the spread of online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The challenge is multi-faceted and requires more than just one solution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I note the terms of reference of the Select Committee set out in the Motion and agree with the same.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I would comment on the reference to possible legislative measures.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This would indeed be a natural and obvious response.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I trust though, that the Government will not only be considering legislative options.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):   The development of digital technology in this era has changed the way we communicate and has an effect on the spread of information.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One of the consequences is the spread of online falsehoods on an unprecedented scale.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: All types of falsehoods can spread very quickly and its impact on society is quite significant.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: One example is a video that became viral, that purportedly show Muslims in London celebrating the Paris terrorist attack in November 2015.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In reality, the video was a recording of a group of people celebrating Pakistan’s victory in a cricket match.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: This hoax has further stoked anger and hatred towards Muslims after the Paris incident.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Just imagine if a similar situation happens in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Race relations in Singapore may become fractured and the lives of our multi-racial and multi-religious society will be affected.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Therefore, it is important that we act quickly to prevent the spread of online falsehoods.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The current efforts are inadequate to resolve this problem.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The problem of online falsehoods cannot be resolved by a single group.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The Government, tech companies, media, society – they must all play their part.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, I support this Motion.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am very glad that the Government has put up this Motion to call for setting up of a Select Committee on Deliberate Online Falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I applaud the Government for taking this approach because this is a very important issue, affecting every Singaporean, young and old, and hence, a call for extensive and in-depth discussion and deliberation is most important.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We all know that fake news is not anything new.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It has been around since olden times and even now, in present days.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is being used by both state and non-state players to profit, manipulate, divide and to conquer.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In 2017, Minister Shanmugam, in replying Members of the House, identified three situations of such things.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And I would quote him: "Genuine feedback – it could be in error where the person could have made a mistake but genuine, well-intentioned feedback or complaints because there is a difference of viewpoints, allegations based on an honest belief in certain facts; that is one category.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Generally, there should be no consequences for that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The second category where the complaint is justified, feedback is justified and we must take action.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The third category is what the Member is focused on, which is false, deliberate, malicious allegations.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We are not talking about errors, we are talking about deliberate falsehoods, malice." And so, I would look forward to the Select Committee to look especially into this third category that the Minister has mentioned and examine deeply the consequences of these falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the UK, there was a call for submission on the understanding of fake news by the British parliament.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And, on the website, you can see that parliament actually wants the British public to define what is fake news.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The second thing which I thought is really important is, I quote, "Where does biased but legitimate commentary shade into propaganda and lies?" I think this second point is very important for the Select Committee to look at.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Because this Government has been advocating for more active citizenry, hoping that Singaporeans would be more involved in discourse and discussions.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen more Singaporeans speaking up and, of course, the social media has provided that platform for them to express their views.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Where the media is concerned, for example, should there be a responsible journalism defence?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Thus, if a media outlet acts responsibly before publishing a story, for example, by conducting inquiries into whether an incident did in fact happen, and by approaching the authorities for a comment, should it be free from liability even if it later turns out that the story contains some inaccuracies?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Also, provided that the media has made such inquiries, if it is merely reporting what someone else says without endorsing what has been said, should it be free from liability?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Green Paper mentioned – and just now Minister Yaacob also mentioned –the case of the TRS incident.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The relevant authorities have moved swiftly and under the existing laws, dealt with that issue.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Based on this, we should start our discussion on whether we need new legislation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I am not saying that these Acts are perfect and do not require review.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, some of these laws give very broad powers to the authorities, and it may be that they should themselves be reviewed but to ensure that the interests of individuals that I have mentioned previously are properly recognised.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But one of the concerns about online platforms is that news would spread so quickly.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, when there is a falsehood being put up, how do we respond as swiftly?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And to act swiftly and to respond swiftly, we just cannot depend only on law enforcers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: No matter how tough the law is, any person with intention to sabotage with fake news or falsehood would still do it, for profit or for malice.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To stop the spreading of news, it needs the citizens to be vigilant, to take up responsibility but not to vigilante.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, in this age of social media, the people's responsibility then, must include the ability to discern and make up their mind what news are dubious and what are falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Any good literacy programme must be taught critically so that those who are learning it will learn how to think critically.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, I hope the Select Committee will look at how to further our media literacy outreach, and not just going to schools, but to workplaces, community and grassroots sites.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But I also that this is a wonderful opportunity for everyone to start thinking about these issues, and to ride on the work of the Select Committee that will gain public attention, that the Government should consider, at the same time, put out sustainable engagement programmes on media literacy at all of these sites that I have just mentioned.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As the world become more complex, no one person or institution, can claim to hold truth, to have all information.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, everyone contribute to providing information to help to discover truths and to fact-check.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Fake news preys on the confirmation biasness of its readers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And so, as it travels very quickly, unsuspecting public would be taken in very quickly.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, to help public learn to discern truths, facts and opinions from lies and falsehoods, it is important that there is a high level of transparency of information flowing especially, from authority.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And finally, Rebecca Solnit, in her book "Hope in the Dark" talks about how ordinary people that appear in Superhero movies produced by Hollywood are always portrayed to be passive, clueless, cowardly and helpless, because without the clueless public, Superheroes cannot perform their tasks.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: But in real life, we realise that people are not that clueless.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: And I think, in the fighting of online falsehoods, we need all people to be responsible – the people, the Government, the media, the civil society, because we really cannot wait for Superheroes in those crisis moments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have three points – all three points support the intention to refer the issue of deliberate online falsehoods to a Select Committee.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: First, even as we try to tackle the problem of deliberate online falsehoods upstream, to be truly inoculated to the adverse impacts of falsehoods, people need discernment to differentiate between truth and falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, the repudiation of an article as false is often announced hours after the viral impact and seldom reaches all the audiences.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: False news may also continue to circulate making the article that repudiated it seem outdated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That survey showed that Singaporeans who are more optimistically biased tend to "evaluate the news they receive on social media as less credible" and that they "tend to search for more information".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This scepticism that leads people to dig deeper is encouraging.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Nevertheless, the value of repetition and perceived corroboration may pose difficulty with automated accounts and multiple websites putting up the same unreliable information.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, even as people need to disbelieve falsehood, they need to be able to discern what is true, what is reliable.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An article entitled "US kids suss out the truth about fake news" by Washington Post and later picked up by The Straits Times had this to say, I quote, "While they once feared teenagers would fall for everything they read online, now teachers are increasingly concerned that their students will grow up not believing anything they read – or worse, believing the difference between what is real and what is fake is a matter of choice." That would be dangerous.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is important is discernment and not just disbelief.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, empowering people to discern between truth and lies is of paramount importance.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Only then can we increase our resistance to the insidiousness of falsehood.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Though the phenomenon of "fake news" is not a new 21st century phenomenon but more like an upgraded or multiplied upgraded version of rumours, the rise of technology has exacerbated the issue.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In an age of increasing technology sophistication, artificial intelligence can fabricate a scenery that had not existed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is possible to make a video showing Barack Obama saying things he did not actually say – all without compromising the perceived authenticity of the video, a point alluded to by Minister Yaacob in his speech.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even without sophisticated technology, a simple deliberate miscaptioning and hence, repurposing of an old picture or video, can paint a very misleading picture.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Using an apparently trustworthy news article but adding unverified and misleading facts can turn groups of people against each other.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When that happens, the corroboration of articles seems to enhance the perceived credibility of the article rather than expose its falsehood.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Other ways to increase the audience reach and strengthen perceived veracity by enhancing popularity are through automated bots and phantom accounts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Social media has also become a platform for individuals and larger entities to transcend traditional territorial boundaries to irresponsibly wield the sword of the keyboard to manipulate politics, destabilise a country, increase polarisation or to simply get rich.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Internet has enabled a cloak of anonymity to increase the lack of accountability and enable an easy masquerade of a credible news site through subtle changes to a website domain.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While it is not easy, tackling deliberate online falsehoods is important for our future as a nation, for our future as a democracy, for our future as "one united people".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Allow me, Sir, to move on to my second point: falsehoods can divide us but we need to stand united − united as one multiracial Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Unity is important, and unity can be threatened by false allegations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In that instance, the purported victims were repainted as the oppressors, exploiting the tension in Myanmar towards the Rohingyas.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These examples show how false allegations can target and wrongfully exacerbate society’s fault lines and threaten unity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There needs to be space to clarify misconceptions, address prejudices and reduce misinformation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Truth is the antidote to lies, and lies need to be addressed in order to dispel suspicions based on falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: People who tell the truth do not need to and should not be afraid of the actions to be taken.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I repeat: people who tell the truth do not need to and should not be afraid of the actions that will be taken.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There is a difference, of course, between falsehoods and truths that we do not like to hear.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Green Paper is entitled "Deliberate Online Falsehoods".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is important for a democracy to work that ideas be exchanged.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: However, concocting a collage out of unrelated data, then squeezing an untenable conclusion out of it and then attempting to pass off that conclusion as truth − now, that is dangerous and should be avoided.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Simply put, there is no interest in being misinformed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially so when important decisions have to be made.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, while we should not hamper constructive discussion and the expression of viewpoints, we need to make sure that decisions are based on the foundation of truth and not the shifting sands of falsehood.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What would happen if such important decisions were made based on these false premises?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If voters acted on this, the electoral process by which democracy is effected would not function as it was meant to be.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, we need to act − and we need to act now.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen how polarising the effects can be in countries like the United States (US) and France in recent years.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: We have also had our own share of fake news occurrences in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I reached out quickly to a trusted contact in MCI who immediately assured me that the story was, indeed, fake.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: However, what astonished me was how quickly this piece of "fake news" spread and the alarm it caused.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I can only imagine the distress caused to those who know the Minister.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This incident, and many others like it, tell us that online falsehoods or fake news is a phenomenon that is not going to go away.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Indeed, it is going to be more prevalent as the world becomes digital and reliant on social media and online platforms for news.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: So, how do we combat this phenomenon, knowing that it is something that we cannot control?

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: One of the areas that the Government and the community have to work on is creating multiple credible platforms to push out accurate information, corrections and rebuttals.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The Singapore Government has 16 Ministries and 61 Statutory Boards − and I am not even including Government-linked companies here.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Each Ministry and Statutory Board has its own website and social media channels.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In confronting fake news that is viral and in danger of triggering a nationwide panic, there must be an immediate response across all channels to ensure that the accurate information drowns out the fake news.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Mainstream news media outlets can help lead this charge by enhancing their credibility.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: At a Digital Media Conference in November last year, The Straits Times Editor and Editor-in-Chief of the Singapore Press Holdings' English, Malay and Tamil Media Group, Mr Warren Fernandez, said, "Societies have to find a way to make sure that good content gets out there because if you don’t do anything about it, bad content will drive out good content".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I agree completely with this point, and feel strongly that newsrooms of today can do a lot more.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: One could make the argument that most Singaporeans get their news in real time from platforms like Facebook because even the mainstream news media today get their news and videos from Facebook.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: But I believe that this can change with more robust and credible news gathering and reporting.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While we all know that our very own Prime Minister Lee is one of the biggest social media influencers in Singapore because of the sheer number of followers across his social media channels, there are others who also have a wider reach.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: For us to combat fake news with immediacy and magnitude, it is critical that we engage as many credible influencers as possible.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The other approach which the Committee could focus on is education.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: I was pleased to read this week that tertiary institutions in Singapore are taking up the fight against fake news.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: While that is a great start, I feel that the education has to start at a much earlier stage − at preschool.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: If you go to any restaurant or hawker centre in Singapore today, toddlers watching content on iPads and mobile phones are the norm.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Most kids learn to use iPads and mobile phones even before they learn how to speak.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Sadly, when my son was growing up, these devices were not available.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: In this digital age, parents and teachers need to teach kids about the difference between what is "fake" and what is "true".

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: It is akin to teaching our children not to talk to strangers.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: To be able to tell the difference between what is fake and what is true has to be ingrained in kids from young.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This is not something that can be solved by legislation.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: This needs a whole-of-Singapore approach – everyone from parents to grandparents to teachers need to get involved.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Lastly, there is a need for the small group of influencers out there who take pride in offering alternative views and commentary on political and social happenings in Singapore to be more factual, accurate and constructive.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Their opinions may not necessarily be fake, but their views and opinions can be very damaging to our social and cultural fabric.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: These influencers are Singaporeans, many of whom are very familiar with the out-of-bounds (OB) markers as they may be experts or former media professionals.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these influencers may contribute commentaries to foreign online publications that are written to deliberately elicit a strong reaction.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: The community should be wary of these influencers, and learn to seek other credible sources of information before making a judgement.

speaker: Mr Ganesh Rajaram (Nominated Member)
text: Fake news is a very serious phenomenon, and, if left unchecked, will have disastrous consequences for our social fabric.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This is an insightful slogan of Washington Post, a well-regarded US newspaper.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The Washington Post recognises that a democracy cannot survive and thrive without an informed public discourse informed by facts, truth and transparency.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, in the past few years, leading democracies have been hacked.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The long list includes the US, UK, France, Germany, Sweden and Italy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: These nations have been hacked by foreign powers and special interest groups, who systematically inject fake news into the openness and the connectedness of many democracies, so as to further their foreign agenda or narrow interests and, in certain instances, they have succeeded.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Why do such concerted efforts frequently succeed, even in mature democracies with well-informed electorates?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We are beginning to benefit from new research on fake news.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In short, few pieces of fake news survive, but those that do, go viral.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We should not be surprised by the ingenuity of these algorithms, because social media companies have an overriding financial interest to keep us entertained and connected for as many hours a day as possible, by delivering one dopamine dose, one newsfeed at a time.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Fake news also thrives because of our psychological make-up.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Psychologists have noted that for the human mind to critically examine whether an article is true or false, a person must first mentally articulate them, temporarily accepting the news as possibly true.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But even if our brain subsequently rule what we read as fake, our mind has already made a subconscious note of that, and this lingers in our minds longer than we think it does.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Merely seeing a newsfeed headlines many times, even if they are later debunked as fake news, make it more credible than it should.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In short, even if we recognise news as fake, fake news can influence us subtly.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: People might speculate as to the reasons for the Select Committee.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, it has been suggested that one of the reasons for convening this Select Committee is the petition process which was initiated by some activists in relation to Parliament’s consideration and adoption of the Administration of Justice (Protection) Bill in August 2016.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: But such speculation does not change the issue at hand.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the formation of the Selection Committee, I have two other suggestions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: One, while the Committee’s work is critical, we should tackle the issue upstream by strengthening our people’s understanding of how our society works.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Any country with an under-informed electorate has fertile grounds for fake news to thrive.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, we must find more effective ways to keep our people well-informed about the fundamentals of how our society works.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: This includes how our society manages our multi-cultural and multi-religious fault-lines; how the Government spends its money, and how we manage our reserves; how our political and electoral process functions; how we encourage transparency in public debate among Singaporeans, but also saying no to foreign influence on our public opinion.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A good way to start is to teach them in schools.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Today, we already teach critical thinking in schools, and we do have social studies and national education.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: So, I agree with Mr Kok Heng Leun's view on strengthening media literacy.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: When I meet young citizens, I sometimes ask them how do they build their world-view and what is their source of news.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: More and more, I am hearing that they are increasingly relying on news from social media or WhatsApp-sharing.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: A clear understanding on the news consumption patterns will be necessary to help us calibrate policies, so that we can create a healthy balance between healthy discourse and necessary intervention.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Public discourse is the means for our society to reflect collectively, reflect on what values matter, reflect on whether our policies have lived up to our ideals, and reflect on whether we have pushed a logical idea to its illogical extreme.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For the longest time, our mainstream media has served as an accurate mirror for our society to reflect upon.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With the rise of social media and the decline of mainstream media, many Singaporeans are no longer even looking at the same mirror.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, vested or financial interests distort their social media newsfeeds more and more each day.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: In the decades ahead, we have a lot of major decisions to make.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And we need to collectively decide on our way forward on the basis of facts, and not rumours and, certainly, not fake news.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We must do everything in our power to combat fake news to ensure that Singapore’s public deliberations continue to be enlightened because democracy dies in darkness.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: With that, Mr Deputy Speaker, I stand in full support of the Motion.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is imperative for the Committee to study this issue in depth and solicit responses from the public and various interest groups as a ground-up inclusive move, as compared to introducing legislation alone without consultation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Online platforms could create tools to help stem the spread of falsehoods.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Technical steps could be taken to remove or limit access to propaganda outlets using the conditions of use of most Internet service providers and "report/block content" buttons.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I suggest that an online platform be created for public to complain about factual inaccuracies and to check the validity of the news.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Currently, the Ministry of Health (MOH) has an online platform to feedback on specific concerns or complaints with the healthcare service providers or the Ministry.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: There could be an additional category to include feedback on online falsehoods relating to public health safety issues for MOH to investigate and clarify with members of the public.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is one such example I could give and other Ministries could also have a similar kind of arrangement.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This would mobilise the public energies to police lies and distortions with a web-based open system listing journalists, publications, news channels and other websites.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Given the diverse demographic of our Republic, it is important to embrace diverse viewpoints.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Singapore Conversations was a good way to engage Singaporeans openly on policies and the rationale behind them.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Government could continue to sharpen their strategic communication efforts and media activities to be able to rebut false stories and to be believed, and it has to be responsive and timed.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is a very important topic that many Members have also spoken about.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, the focus could be on educating our citizens on media and digital information literacy.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Secondary schools could also include media and digital information literacy in their curriculum, where students learn to pick on cues to uncover misinformation, question misleading sources and resist the temptation of believing just simply.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Eventually, we hope to cultivate a generation with a healthy scepticism on the online information.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should monitor the situation and consider various effective means of curbing and preventing deliberate on-line falsehood.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Legislation and tighter controls must also be considered to combat the “virus” of falsehood.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: As for foreign influence, we need to have some gate-keeping mechanism to know the source of the news, who is the sponsor, what is the intent of the action, as what the Minister for Law has mentioned earlier.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should learn from the experiences of other countries and study what actions have been taken to overcome those challenges.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: France, Germany and the US are also similarly working to overcome the problem of fake news.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Similarly, in Germany, legislation allows for fake news or illegal content in social network to be removed within 24 hours.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In concluding, my belief is that the Select Committee appointment is a step in the right direction and I support this move.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair again at 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Deputy Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 3.55 pm until 4.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: One way to think about today's debate is whether we should adopt a paternalistic or a liberal stance towards false information per se – whether online or off.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think our discussion today should take bearing from the existing principles that already inform this House's views on falsehoods and truths – namely, the relatively uncontroversial principles that we should, first, reduce falsehoods as much as we can and, second, promote the truth as vigorously as we can.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But as with so much in policy making, this is easier said than done.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Deliberate Online Falsehoods cut across these two broad spectrums: (a) completely false information, photos or videos purposefully created and spread to confuse or misinform; (b) information, photos or videos manipulated to deceive, or old photographs shared as new.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: More than half of British users of social media surveyed have admitted that they fail to check the original source of online material before sharing or "liking" it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Most of us admit that we cannot distinguish the truth from falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: New processes are needed because the status quo is based on two assumptions which we now know to be questionable.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: First, the assumption of infinite, or even adequate, time and capacity to process information.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There might be one camp choosing to oppose this motion who may think "here we go again – mollycoddling us by restricting information for our sakes".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Freedom of information has a nice ring to it, and restricting freedom always requires justification. "Don't treat us like little children", they say, unable to distinguish between truths and falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And, indeed, the argument from freedom goes further – even if we do make mistakes, it is our mistake to make.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, the Government should not – and should not want to – protect us from our mistakes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Surely, it is a fundamental tenet of our democratic system that people should be allowed to make their own decisions, and if those decisions are mistaken, it is a matter of accepting the outcome of a democratic process.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But it is also true that people have a right to expect that the political leaders that they have put in place carry a duty – to ensure that their decision making environment – that is, the people's decision-making environment – is not populated by intentional falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: That their leaders not be blind to the dangers that such falsehoods can have on freedom of opinions, religions, races and genders.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Also, it should be noted that we are restricting fraudulent information and not restricting information per se.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In fact, I see countering falsehoods as a way to safeguard freedom of speech – by ensuring the conditions are in place for there to be meaningful and free debate.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Falsehoods mislead, crowd out truths and prevent constructive debate and discourse.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Just throwing all the "data" we have into a pot and then leaving people to distinguish between good and bad information makes the assumption that people have both the time and the capacity to do this.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I do not mean "capacity" in the strict sense of expertise or education – I mean it in the loose sense of "inclination" – or whether we "can be bothered." Indeed, most people cannot be bothered.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In 2007, FairPrice filed a police report after we found a picture of "halal pork", allegedly sold by stores, on the Internet.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If the first person who saw this checked with us and deleted it, it would have died there.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Instead, the news was carried in both the mainstream media as well as online news media, and caused a stir in the community, and rightly so.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It was so widespread that Majlis Ugama Islam Singapura (MUIS) had to carry out physical checks.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It went viral again in 2011 and again in 2014, and FairPrice had to respond publicly that this was a 2007 hoax that had resurfaced.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Even today, 10 years later, I still get messages asking me about this.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, for the last time, I hope, this is a deliberate online falsehood!

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, a lie can travel half way around the world before the truth gets out of bed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Last year, too, the Agri-Food and Veterinary Authority (AVA) had to step in and come out to debunk a Facebook video that alleged a coffee shop in Ang Mo Kio was selling "man-made eggs from China".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: False information will be the Pope's theme for his annual World Communications Day in 2018.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think, if the Pope deems falsehoods harmful enough to cause "polarisation" of public opinion, all the more should Singapore urgently formulate recommendations to curb the peddling of misinformation, the chaos and the additional costs it brings.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We know of instances of brands' reputations tarnished by appearing on fake news websites and, unwittingly, funding their activities.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Back in March last year, Havas Group UK, a media agency, decided to stop all its ad spending on Google and YouTube after ads for its clients appeared next to "questionable or unsafe content" online.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Consequences go beyond dollars and cents into the very destiny of men.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the UK, voters for remain or exit voted on the basis of information later found to be false.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Countries are hoping to sway online citizens to be one way or the other, vote one way or the other, pressure their governments one way or the other, using – not evidence or facts, but by casting fear, seeding doubt, and pressing emotional buttons.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There are many of us who do not have the knowledge nor the time to sieve through falsehoods; this is exacerbated by the mode of delivery of such news.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: How easy it is to like, comment or share information these days.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We owe a duty of care to the public, by presenting them with straight facts, we owe it to each other to be vigilant of misinformation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to be vigilant and alert to decipher masses of information thrown at them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We know this in the same way we know it is bad to eat too much sugar, that exercise is good and sloth bad.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We know and yet we do not do what we should; instead, quite often, we do what we should not.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, we need the vigilance of laws, regulations and due process.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We need to educate the community, let them know if the news comes from a certified source, and equip them to decide whether to read or share it.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, we owe it to them, to ourselves to ensure that the environment under which such decision making takes place is as uncluttered with falsehoods as possible.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Having regulations and due process also reduces our hiding behind the excuse of "honest mistakes".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We make claims, and then, when proven false, we apologise and say, "we are all human".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We did not intend to mislead, to misrepresent, our memories are faulty, and blah, blah, blah.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Intentions aside, we all know that the consequences matter.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Having a review of how we regard such falsehoods will raise the bar for due care in public discourse, and also, hopefully, reduce the instances of being reckless with the truth.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We are all imperfect beings – and, hence, need to show that we have taken due care when we engage in public debates.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If Singapore had four seasons, I would say winter is coming.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Those who follow Game of Thrones, "winter is coming".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Given that the assumption of infinite time and capacity is false, our first principle must be to reduce falsehoods as much as we can, to be vigilant and guard against the purveyors of such harmful things.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In short: False assumption 1 – people have infinite time and capacity to make decisions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, Principle 1 is – reduce falsehoods as much as we can.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But there is a deeper objection, Mr Deputy Speaker, about regulation of information.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It argues that a Government does not have a right to decide beforehand what is true and what is false.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: That people have a right to all the facts, and if one set of fact is proved wrong, only then will they decide to change their decisions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This is the argument from the "marketplace of ideas" – that people will change their minds when the facts change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As Cicero, the great Roman orator said, "Does not, as fire dropped upon water is immediately extinguished and cooled, so, does not, I say, a false accusation, when brought in contact with a most pure and holy life, instantly fall and become extinguished?" Cicero, I think, did not have experience with "halal pork"!

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The answer to his question, whether falsehoods wither and die when exposed to the light of truth is, of course, no!

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Lies thrive and contest against the truth, even when the "truth" is as evident as where a man was born, or the amount of money spent on healthcare.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the post-truth world, the role of facts, unfortunately, has been shown to have less force then supposed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Instead of changing their minds when presented with a different set of facts, people may instead choose to disregard these facts or find ways to find new facts which support their pre-existing ideas.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This confirmation bias is well-tested and should be taken into consideration when we make the marketplace argument.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Stronger fact-checking/ self-regulation by social media sites and technology companies.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Popular search engines and social media platforms, such as Google and Facebook, have been struggling for years to fight false news, despite their best intentions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
