text: For instance, in the wake of the Las Vegas shooting last October, despite Facebook and Google promising to inhibit such circulation, falsehoods, such as the identity and the affiliation of the shooter, still ran rampant.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is much room for improvement, especially when one reason is that the algorithm in these systems often bring attention to posts that get their readers' interests – exactly what falsehood is designed to do.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: If the post garnered 10,000 likes and shares, then, surely, it must be real, right?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: And this is where numbers provide false safety.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There is very little wisdom in crowds, or, at least, very little that we ought to take at face value when it comes to important decisions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is understandable that many people do not have the time, resources or energy to recognise and safeguard against falsehoods, before believing or sharing with others.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yet, self-policing in this manner is very much dependent on the ability of individuals to spot such news, to begin with.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Another challenge is the need for individuals to recognise that they need to be socially responsible: Think before sharing.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The limitations to public education now are in its outreach and time.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It will be difficult to reach certain segments of the community, such as the elderly.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Also, public education of this nature takes a long time before results bear fruit, and we do need some immediate solutions, given the gravity of the situation now.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the UK, the Culture, Media and Sport Select Committee is conducting an inquiry into "fake news".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Facebook and Twitter may face sanctions if they fail to hand over information to the Committee to assist in a Parliamentary investigation into Russian interference in the EU referendum.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: This achieves the crucial objective of deterrence, which non-regulatory measures mentioned above cannot achieve.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: The extent of Government involvement requires deep discussion.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We may end up freezing free speech online.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Legislation, if overly relied on, may also weaken the ability of society to educate themselves and discern what is real or not for themselves.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is clear that the challenges brought by deliberate online falsehoods are many and complex.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: You will notice, Mr Deputy Speaker, that I have merely challenged two assumptions and reinforced two principles in the wake of these false assumptions.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I have stressed the role of process in ensuring that the environment for our public discourse remains clean and unencumbered.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As to the actual processes themselves – what they should be, how much is needed – I think these are the issues that the Select Committee is best placed to explore, as it allows the committee to draw representations from contributors and stakeholders of all sectors.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In particular, I think such a committee would also be able to articulate more clearly and in greater detail the principles that underline our governance model in terms of regulating information.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It is not just a balance, but a difference between means and ends.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We do not pursue freedom for its own end.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: We do not, if I may put it bluntly, have a “philosophy of freedoms”.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As Mr S Rajaratnam, our then Minister for Foreign Affairs, said in a speech to foreign correspondents, “We see freedom of the press not as the end, but as means to an all-embracing end – the integrity and independence of our country – its security, its prosperity, the eradication of anything that would sow seeds of social, racial and religious conflicts which is the rule rather than the exception in the world today.” Sir, he was speaking in 1986.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Yes, more than 30 years ago – and the world has come full circle.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, I think we ought to hear his words to the end.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: He said, “Singapore has far more vulnerabilities than most national states because it has none of the essential prerequisites for a viable, stable and prosperous state.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: It has nevertheless functioned fairly adequately for 27 years only on the basis of two intangibles – ideas and the human characters shaped by these ideas.” Ideas as shaped by human character, not ideas as tossed willy nilly into a pot, undiscerned, half-formed, half-baked.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Let us all recognise the need to work out for ourselves in Singapore what is the correct approach towards preventing and combating deliberate online falsehoods.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If you apply this presumption to the Internet, it is basically that if something goes viral, that news must have veracity.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The old presumption that if people are all talking about something or sharing some information by the Internet that is going to be true is now the reverse presumption – it is likely something you have to look at very carefully.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Weaponised in this way, deliberate online falsehoods or misinformation can sow societal discord, as has been observed in the Green Paper by the Ministers and in various jurisdictions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Fake news also risks, importantly, devaluing and delegitimising the voices of expertise and the concept of objective data – which undermines society’s ability to engage in a rational discourse based upon shared facts.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As an academic, there is an importance of objective data that is extremely important.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Not just from the Government, not just from a whole-of-Government, but it is has to be a whole-of-Singapore approach.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Select Committee should in my view, Sir, should consider four points, as I would set out in this speech.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Two, how do we utilise the Government's existing toolbox of soft measures as well as hard laws to combat fake news?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Three, how do we equip users of the Internet, most of Singaporeans, to be the first line of defence against online falsehoods?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And finally, how could we involve major Internet platforms or ICT companies in our efforts to combat this problem?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Looking at the definition, as the first point, it is important to clarify, and for the Select Committee to look into this point, as to what the term ‘"fake news" or deliberate online falsehoods really mean and to frame the problem we are seeking to tackle.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: That phrase fake news for a variety of reasons and for a variety of people is a loaded term capable of being co-opted by different constituents across the world for different purposes.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I note that three professors from NTU have directed their minds to this problem of what is fake news in an article they published in August.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They undertook an examination of 34 scholarly articles and looked at a duration between 2003 and 2017 in order to map the different conceptions of fake news.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They have gone on to say that fake news has two elements.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The first, obviously, would be whether there or not is veracity, or facticity in their view; and secondly, the intention behind the news, the degree to which the author of fake news intends to deceive.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: This would be the most dangerous elements of fake news for online falsehoods.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: When looking at this definition, it is important also to see what it would exclude.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, as an example, fictitious news stories with a vague plausibility but which are aimed at humour should be excluded if they are deliberately satirical and that they caveat that that is their purpose.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: If there is innocent, inadvertent inaccuracies or mistakes, as some have spoken about earlier, that should be excluded.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And finally, impassioned opinion or commentary that is based on facts, even if people would disagree with these facts, that should be excluded.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Ultimately, it is important for the Select Committee to give us a parameter of what is fake news that we would be looking at.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The Select Committee should outline and recommend how a Smart Nation in the 21st century should responsibly enforce existing norms.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: There is a considerable range in this tool box, which regulators have.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It ranges from inspection, support, advice and it can be backed by criminal, civil and reputational sanctions.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Where damage or harm is caused, appropriate remedies are currently available, as some Members have spoken about in the Defamation Act, the Sedition Act, the Maintenance of Religious Harmony Act and various steep fines that the IMDA can impose.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Beyond what currently exists, the Select Committee should be thinking about what is necessary to be part of the arsenal that is currently not there but that should be there because it is necessary to be there.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Third, how do we equipping Internet users, regular Singaporeans to be that first line of defence?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: According to a research paper by IT security company Trend Micro in May last year, Trend Micro said this "In a post-truth era, news is easy to manufacture but challenging to verify, it’s essentially up to the users to better discern the veracity of the stories they read and prevent fake news from further proliferating".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: I would therefore agree with the Members who have spoken before me to talk about the importance of discerning truth from fake news.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is far more difficult than you would think.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As a very simple example, those of us who follow football can understand that if you have a WhatsApp chat group, there is information on your sports teams, on the players that you support and what you think should be changed.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Should the managers be doing something different, should a new player be acquired and very often fake news is actually propagated on these WhatsApp chat groups.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: People are upset, but how far is that damage?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, I would not look at that particular example as something that we should come up with a very strong enforcement measure against.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: How much of this is fake news and what is the damage of that fake news, is also something we should look at.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: There is a need to appreciate the difference in the way people of different ages, social backgrounds and genders use and respond to fake news.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Some groups, Sir, are more vulnerable than others.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Outreach to the elderly could be done through community ambassadors and role models who vet these WhatsApp messages that are sent that could alarm them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Online deliberate falsehoods, Sir, in my opinion are a poison.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The same networks that false news has benefited from could also be applied as an antidote to this poison.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Fact-checkers, who are perhaps journalists, university students, scholars to look into information before it is widely disseminated or to constantly correct misinformation as it happens.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Campaigns should be launched to raise awareness on the scourge of misinformation and to equip these fact-checkers with the tools needed to combat falsehoods.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps we could look at having a repository of information that is truthful when fake news is actually propagated on a wide scale.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Major Internet platforms should support the research and development of appropriate technological solutions to disinformation and propaganda which users may apply on a voluntary basis.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: They should cooperate with initiatives that offer fact-checking services to users and review their advertising models to ensure that they do not adversely impact diversity of opinions that users can hold.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: It is important not to put the entire burden of policing on these platforms on the people, on the users who are using them.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: As one example, I look to a colleague at SMU, Prof Warren Chik, who has come out to say and written in the Law Gazette that it may be appropriate not always to have new legislation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: So, yes, have some soft laws, have guidelines, have best practices but should we go straight into legislation?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: Prof Chik also says that it would be important to clarify with the relevant Internet intermediaries hosting or providing access to information to come under the ambit of existing regulations overseen by the IMDA.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: He said that making it clear that the regime covers news aggregators, social media platforms that provide newsfeeds and other similar content hosts or sources of news will have the effect of ensuring compliance with combating deliberate online falsehoods and concomitant amendments to the regulations to include specific conditions for operation.

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: What are the benefits of legislation on this particular point?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And if there is going to be legislation, will there be aspects of that legislation which are not just hardcoding new crimes but is giving support to vulnerable and the youth to raise awareness against fake news?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: The question, therefore, for the Select Committee is: is technological design currently being harnessed to both promote more credible content or present content in a way that fosters consumer scepticism and critical analysis?

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: And this "winter", I am not talking about seasons, but of course, "winter" from the Game of Thrones; that "winter is coming".

speaker: Asst Prof Mahdev Mohan (Nominated Member)
text: But I think what we should do is to say, "Well, if there is winter is coming, how do we insulate ourselves, and get the thickest coats and the best protection from this winter?" Because usage of the Internet is not going to stop, it is only going to increase.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: While there are many aspects of this discussion, I would like to focus on two important considerations.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Those who advocate strongly for freedom of speech are quick to argue that the "market" should be left to "correct" misinformation and disinformation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They point out that a marketplace of ideas and thoughts will certainly eventually lead to the truth emerging.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This, while true in the past, may not necessarily be the case in this digital era, where falsehoods are propagated at such speeds and volumes which makes it difficult for the common man to discern between fact and fiction.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this digital era, algorithms and social media platforms can also be manipulated by motivated parties – local and foreign, private and state-payers.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Measures need to be taken to ensure that while free speech is exercised, facts will prevail.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Free speech must be founded on facts, and not on falsehoods, especially those that are designed to undermine society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The dangers of how freedom of speech can be abused to cause significant harm to society, can be seen from the experiences in the UK and Australia.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the UK, online falsehoods were used to distort sentiment in relation to government policies and to breed xenophobia.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: False information was also used to stir up racial tensions in the UK to smear Muslims as a group, and to turn non-Muslims against Muslims.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the face of numerous occurrences of online falsehoods in the UK, the UK government has launched a parliamentary inquiry into fake news.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their experiences have shown them that if left unchecked, the spread of falsehoods has a serious detrimental impact on society.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Australia, online falsehoods were used to stir up racial tensions to smear Muslims as a group and to stir up xenophobic feelings.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Conducted largely through the social media and online networks, Australian anti-Islamic groups demanded companies that carry halal certification labels to drop them.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This was part of what were known as rallies to "reclaim Australia".

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There was never any evidence to support the allegation that money from halal certification funded terrorist groups.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Just like the UK, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission has undertaken a formal inquiry into major digital platforms and their impact on media, journalism and advertising, with the impact of falsehoods as part of this inquiry.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Australian process is somewhat similar to Singapore’s proposed Select Committee process, in that it is formally convened to study a problem and has powers to obtain evidence and hold hearings.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The second consideration is that falsehoods have the ability to radicalise individuals with extremist sentiments.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Terrorist groups have long recognised the need to use online media effectively, in order to radicalise masses and achieve their sinister aims.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In an undated letter to Taliban leader Mullah Omar, quoted in 2014, Al-Qaeda’s then leader Osama bin Laden himself observed that "90 percent of the preparation for war is effective use of the media".

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Al-Qaeda was long advocating ghazwa ma’lumatiyya, or information operations, and harb electroniyya which is electronic warfare.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Bin Laden’s successor, Ayman al-Zawahiri, shared this same view.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: He referred to "jihad of the bayan" which is the message of declaration, and considered this more important than "jihad of the spear" – he praised the "knights of the media jihad", and the "clandestine mujahideen" who were conducting it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Terrorist organisations use Twitter to put out fake news stories.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: There have been many instances of mainstream media mistaking terrorist-originated tweets as legitimate sources of breaking news.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: An example of a terrorist organisation that has been using online falsehoods to push its own agenda is the Islamic State (ISIS).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Their goal as jihadists was to blame the West and the Americans.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Iraq military and the US military released counter-footage, trying to show the truth of the matter, but objective truth has little meaning as the followers of ISIS cannot be swayed by evidence.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, even if you put the counter-truth, it is hard to sway the public and hard to counter the perceptions the mistruths have already shaped.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, we need to be aware of the consequences when our online space is hijacked or influenced by players with certain motivations or agenda.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In our multi-religious and multi-ethnic Singapore, which has enjoyed decades of stability and harmony, such falsehoods should have no place as someone with the intention to stir up emotions and they can do it easily, using religion.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What measures do we need the Government to look into?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And these are some suggestions, I hope, the Select Committee can consider.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The EU, UK and France are considering similar take-down laws.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: New Zealand takes a different approach under the Harmful Digital Communications Act that allows the Court to order a right to reply or to correct false statements concerning individuals.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Select Committee is therefore a good platform to get views from many Singaporeans and other stakeholders to hear their views, challenges and for us to learn the best way to take this forward for the greater good of Singapore and fellow citizens.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, the Government must also assure Singaporeans that this is not an effort to silence critics and that the citizens must not lose that freedom to critic, feedback and put points of views across, as long as they are based on truths and not deliberately pushing falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Please allow me to continue my speech in Malay.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: (In Malay):  : The move to initiate a Parliamentary process in order to study and obtain feedback on the issue of falsehoods that are deliberately spread online is timely.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is because we have long faced the issue of having all kinds of news and information coming from multiple sources, including from overseas.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What is worrying is that some of these news or information do not state the full picture, or is done out of context.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Another issue pertains to information or news that is spread with a specific agenda.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, during this new year, an ISIS video was spread that showed militants supposedly from Singapore urging ISIS militants from around the world to step up efforts to harm their enemies.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: MUIS and leaders of Malay bodies in Singapore immediately condemned the act of spreading of the video.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I believe that this will not be the last time that such videos and information will be spread.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It will take a continuous effort to prevent the spread of online falsehoods, in addition to efforts to educate and warn our community about the dangers of spreading such news and information.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, terrorist groups have always recognised the need to harness online media effectively in order to propagate their radical beliefs, in addition to recruiting new members to achieve their agenda.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In an undated letter to Taliban leader Mullah Omar that was reported in 2014, the Al-Qaeda leader at that time, Osama bin Laden himself observed that “90% of preparations for war involve the use of media”.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Al-Qaeda have long encouraged what they call ghazwa ma’lumatiyya (or information operations), and harb electroniyya (or electronic warfare).

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Terrorist groups also use Twitter to spread online falsehoods.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In fact, several mainsetream media outlets use information from Twitter as a legitimate source of news that is used in news updates.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: One example pertains to a terrorist organisation that uses online media to spread false information in order to promote their agenda.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A year ago, ISIS claimed that the Al-Nuri In Singapore’s context, as a small multicultural, was destroyed in an airstrike by an allied force led by the US.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, it was ISIS themselves who destroyed the mosque.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Therefore, we must always be wary of the consequence and impact when our online platforms are exploited or influenced by certain groups with their own agenda or motives.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Singapore’s context, as a small multicultural, multi-racial and multi-religious nation, we cannot afford to fall victim to such influences or threats, no matter how small.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is especially so in matters related to religion and race, which are sensitive.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of the sensitive issues being spread, that can heighten emotions and divide our society, are beyond our control because it comes from external sources.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Certain groups will take the opportunity to spread Islamophobia, and this will surely have an impact in terms of our Muslim community’s relationship with non-Muslims and how they view our Muslim community.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Our experience in Singapore, from time to time, is that we are worried whether certain information that is spread and proliferate in social media is incomplete or inaccurate.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Some of these news and information can cause anger or discontent.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, there was an allegation that halal pork was sold at NTUC FairPrice supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: A lot of time and resources were needed to correct such information and give assurance to the public, With technological advancement, information, especially videos and photos, can be created or modified to spread rumours and inaccurate information, and this can spread quickly.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, what are the measures that we would like the Government to study?

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The EU, UK and France are considering similar legislation.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Clearly, the management of online falsehoods is a serious issue.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: We should focus on how Singapore can contain it.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: At the same time, it is hoped that any regulations or laws will not hinder the immense benefits of online platforms and social media technologies that have contributed a lot in terms of spreading information and communications.

speaker: Mr Zaqy Mohamad (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In order to achieve solutions that can benefit everyone, and to protect us from online falsehood, we must support the Select Committee process and recognise the Government’s efforts to take a consultative approach to resolve this sensitive issue.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   In 1969, there were rumours of Malays attacking Chinese in Malaysia.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This led to serious race riots which also affected Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: People of my age or older would have remembered the terror and horror in those few days.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At that time, my family was living in a rubber plantation in the countryside in Malacca.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The houses in the plantation were far away from each other.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the day time, we worked in the plantation; in the evening, the whole family would stay together with our neighbour whose house was far away, for safety reasons.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At that time, my third brother was just born.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I remember my mother told me that if Malays came this evening, we must all quickly escape into the jungle in the back; but we would have to leave our little brother behind.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I was then only eight years old, attending Primary 2.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I understood what my mother meant and felt helpless.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: All I could do was to pray silently that the moment we had to leave our new born brother behind would never come.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For me, those days of fear and anxiety are unforgettable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The 1969 race riots are a case in point to show how rumours and fake news can cause grave damages.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Today, the power of fake news can be even greater.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They spread fast and will affect innocent people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Hence, every Singaporean must stay vigilant and work together to control the spread of fake news.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: First, let us talk about the challenges in discerning truth from falsehood.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Technology can make fake news look more and more credible, almost identical as real news.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As long as there is just one person in the video, this person's image can be matched with different expressions and voices to make it look like the person has actually said those words.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the old days, we used to say “seeing is believing”.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, however, you cannot even believe what you have seen with your own eyes.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In addition to falsehoods in the form of news, there are also computer programmes which can pretend to be a real person and spread rumours online, misleading people to think that many people hold the same view.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Needless to say that fake news spread fast.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Fake news is not only limited to English media.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I often receive fake news in Chinese sent from my residents.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They asked me whether they should believe news, such as Mao Shan Wang durians containing pesticides, plastic rice and fake seaweed.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I noticed that there are many websites and Facebook pages in China, Taiwan and Malaysia that spread fake news.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There are even websites based in Australia targeting at Chinese readers in Singapore.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They publish fake news to stir up trouble for Singapore-China and Singapore-US relationships.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believe that the same phenomenon happens to the Malay and Tamil media as well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Fake news, therefore, can appear in various forms and different languages to influence Singaporeans.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Some people say that a party involved can rebut.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, it shows that the rebuttal tends to be not as “hot” and the transmitting speed is much slower, hence there will still be many people who would believe the fake news.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government cannot know them all and rebut.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because there can be substantial gains behind spreading fake news, it is very difficult to root them out.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How long will that take for most Singaporeans to make?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: They made this money without any effort and conscience, simply by fabricating stories overseas, slandering innocent Singaporeans and dividing our society.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Although the website has been closed down, there are still other similar websites.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Government can find ways to sanction them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Countries can now easily feed fake news to another country.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Now, 150 million is 30 times of our own population.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Fake news can affect the livelihood of a common person, such as a durian seller, simply because of the fake news that durians have pesticides.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Recently, a coffee shop was wrongly accused for selling fake eggs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I believed the owner must have felt helpless and worried.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Fake news can also slow down the transmission of important information and endanger people's safety.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: For example, when Zika was spreading in the US, because some people believed that Zika did not come from mosquitoes but from vaccines or pesticides, they refused to let inspectors check whether there were mosquitoes breeding in their home.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This led to the spread of the virus and many innocent infants and their families being affected.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: There was a lot of fake news circulating in Singapore as well at that time but, luckily, people still believed reliable media and we were able to transmit the right information and control the spread of Zika collectively.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, if we allow fake news to spread and undermine people's trust in reliable media, I am afraid we may not be so lucky the next time.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is not hard to imagine that, for example, a country X would like Singapore to adopt pro-X policies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Like in 1969, they can spread fake news of racial discrimination and marginalisation.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Fake news now can spread to the entire island within hours, stirring up suspicion among races.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Government rebuts but country X is prepared beforehand and a new wave of fake news will surface, accusing the Government of racial discrimination.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Country X will use social media and a large number of messages left by fake accounts to drown the rebuttal from the Government.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In the end, race riots will occur and our economy will slump into recession.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: After that, country X will look for a puppet to set up a political party, proclaiming to protect the interest of a certain race.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The party thereafter manages to acquire political power and adopts pro-X policies.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: X becomes the ultimate beneficiary but the victims are Singaporeans in general.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Those Singaporeans who have forwarded fake news have inadvertently become X’s accomplices.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even superpowers like the US suspect the presence of foreign influence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Small nations like Singapore must also stay vigilant.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope the Committee can pay attention to the following two issues.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Only through an effective Fake News Act can we collectively combat the threats brought by fake news.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We should maintain openness and circulation of information while sanctioning and controlling deliberate falsehoods.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, I hope Singaporeans, including Members of this House, should think twice before forwarding any messages.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Exercise due diligence so that the messages will not end up harming innocent citizens.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, I thank all Members who spoke.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think hon Members ended with a very passionate speech from Er Dr Lee Bee Wah.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Examples have been given of the problems caused by falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Er Lee Bee Wah reminded us about the 1969 race riots caused by rumours of Chinese attacking Malays − examples of real world consequences which have very serious downstream impact for the entire country.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Minister Yaacob talked about the experience his Ministry has had with "The Real Singapore" website − fabricating articles, creating tensions within different racial groups in Singapore − just one example.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Zaqy Mohamed brought up the 2015 Australian example − a misinformation campaign by Australian anti-Islamic groups that halal certification funds terrorism.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Sun Xueling told us of her experience where a false story was spread that the roof of Waterway Terraces I in her ward collapsed.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Within 30 minutes, we had Police and Civil Defence vehicles, all despatched, and resources used up.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Thanaletchimi spoke about the online survey scam relating to NTUC FairPrice that it was rewarding customers with a $500 gift voucher.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Members also spoke about the difficulties we face in responding to falsehoods, and our vulnerability.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Ms Rahayu Mahzam spoke about the difficulty with viral falsehoods, the formation of echo chambers, and the jury is still out on fact-checking mechanisms that Facebook and others have put forward.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr de Souza referred to the danger of proliferation and perceived corroboration through automated accounts and multiple websites putting up the same falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, if it appears in many places, it must true, right?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Henry Kwek referred to the susceptibility to online falsehoods in view of people's psychological make-up, and how falsehoods linger in our minds longer than we think.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Rajaram spoke about how false information will become only more prevalent, not less, as the world becomes more digital.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A number of Members also spoke about possible responses − what this Select Committee ought to consider.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng put out some principles which should guide our response to falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think this is something the Select Committee is explicitly asked to consider.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Methods might change, but we must be clear about the principle, what we are trying to achieve.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah suggested that the Select Committee pay particular attention to whether any measures taken will affect free speech online or silence the critics of the Government.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, keeping falsehoods out of our discourse enables freedom of speech to be meaningfully exercised.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Deliberate falsehoods, I think, have got to be contrasted with factual inaccuracies, resulting in false statements being made.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You can see that they are different, and I assume that that is something that the Select Committee will consider and how we respond, what sort of responses are suggested, may have to take into account the nature of the falsehoods and the intentions behind the falsehoods.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As Mr Kok Heng Leun pointed out, fake news is often used to divide, mislead and conquer society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And he asked how this segues into biased commentary, and I think these are viewpoints that should be made to the Select Committee.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As I have said, strongly held viewpoints but based on inaccuracies is one type of falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the impact on people, what sort of reaction it gets; it is quite different from deliberate, targeted falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: What is the impact of the falsehoods and what sort of reaction, what sort of responses you give to these?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think these are matters that should be considered.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Rajaram called for a multi-pronged approach, including not just legal measures, but also others like public education and digital literacy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He spoke about the need for false information to be counted with immediacy and magnitude to make sure that the accurate response drowns out the falsehood.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
